title: Inside a slice: length, capacity, aliasing
summary: In-place algorithms, full slice expressions and how append really grows.
hints: `ReverseInPlace` and `PartitionEvens` both use two indices walking toward each other: `i, j := 0, len(xs)-1; for i < j { ... }`. In `PartitionEvens`, advance `i` past evens, retreat `j` past odds, and swap when both are stuck. Return `i` (the index of the first odd, or `len(xs)` if there are none).

`FilterInPlace` reuses the input's memory: `out := xs[:0]`, then `for _, x := range xs { if keep(x) { out = append(out, x) } }`. `append` writes into the space you are reading from, always *behind* the read position, so it is safe. `Clip(xs, n)` is the three-index slice `xs[:n:n]`: the last `n` caps the capacity, so a later `append` has to copy instead of overwriting `xs[n]`.

`GrowthCaps(n)`: start with `var s []int` and `last := cap(s)`; append `n` times, and each time `cap(s) != last`, record the new capacity and update `last`. You are watching `append` reallocate. The exact growth numbers belong to the Go runtime; the *shape* (few reallocations, roughly doubling) is the point.
